To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

There is low to very low quality evidence that exercise is not superior to a control intervention in reducing the risk of re-injury, pain, or disability in patients with lateral ankle sprains, plantar fasciitis, or Achilles tendinopathy."

For recent lateral ankle sprains, rehabilitation exercises initiated immediately or one week post injury are effective; for persistent Achilles tendonopathy, eccentric exercises are more effective than an air heel brace, but not as effective as acupuncture; and for plantar heel, static plantar fasciitis stretching provides short term benefit over shockwave therapy.
For recent lateral ankle sprains, immediate rehabilitation exercises may be as effective as delayed rehabilitation exercises.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of exercise on recovery from and the management of soft-tissue injuries of the leg and foot.
the effectiveness of exercise on the recovery and clinical outcomes following leg, ankle, foot injuries.
the effectiveness of exercise in the management of soft-tissue injuries of the leg ankle and foot.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is limited evidence to support the routine use of supervised exercise programs for soft tissue injuries of leg, ankle, foot, and plantar fasciitis.
exercise is not effective for the management of acute ankle sprain, and that it is unclear if exercise is effective for other soft tissue injuries of leg, ankle, foot.
there is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of exercise in the treatment of leg, ankle, foot injuries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
exercise interventions may provide short-term benefits for Achilles tendinopathies and plantar heel pain and that early rehabilitation may be effective for lateral ankle sprain.
there are no strong indications to use exercise as a first line treatment for acute ankle sprains or chronic Achilles tendinopathy.
exercise may be useful in the management of Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis, and lateral ankle sprains but more research is needed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evidence for the effectiveness of exercise interventions is lacking for the management of these soft tissue injuries.
the effectiveness of exercise on soft tissue injuries of leg, ankle, & foot is unclear.
exercise is not a panacea for soft tissue injuries of leg, ankle, foot, but it can be effective for some injuries.
